title: Combination Sum II
prompt:
Given a collection of candidate numbers `candidates` (which may contain duplicates) and a target integer `target`, return all unique combinations of `candidates` where the chosen numbers sum to `target`. Each number in `candidates` may only be used once in a combination.

For deterministic comparison, sort each inner combination in ascending order, and sort the outer list of combinations lexicographically.

examples.explanation: Sorting candidates first ([1,1,2,5,6,7,10]) and skipping repeated values at the same recursion depth avoids duplicate combinations even though 1 appears twice in the input.

hints: This resembles Combination Sum, but each candidate can only be used once and the input can contain duplicate values — both constraints can create duplicate output combinations if handled naively.
Sort candidates first. Using an index that always advances past the current position (not just 'start onward, same index allowed') naturally enforces 'use each element once'.

To avoid duplicate combinations from repeated values, at each recursion level skip a candidate if it equals the previous candidate considered AT THE SAME LEVEL (i.e. i > start and candidates[i] == candidates[i-1]). Prune whenever the sorted candidate exceeds the remaining target, since nothing later in the sorted array can help either.

solution.approach: Sort candidates so equal values are adjacent and pruning by size becomes possible. Backtrack with a forward-only start index, advancing to i+1 on each recursive call (not i, since each element is usable only once). At each level, skip candidates[i] if it equals candidates[i-1] and i > start — this means we already explored including this value at this position and are now trying to skip past it, so re-trying an identical value would just regenerate the same combination. Prune the loop entirely once candidates[i] exceeds the remaining target, since the sorted order guarantees nothing further in the loop can work either. Record the path whenever remaining hits exactly 0.
solution.timeComplexity: O(2^n) worst case, bounded by the branching of the search tree
solution.spaceComplexity: O(n) recursion depth, plus output size
